hints: Focus on what actually happens when $\text{Cl}_2$ dissolves, it does not just stay as $\text{Cl}_2$ in water.
Recall the disproportionation reaction of chlorine with water that forms $\text{HCl}$ and chloric(I) acid, $\text{HClO}$.
Think about which product can act as a strong oxidiser and release to give the hypochlorite ion that disinfects water.
walkthrough:
**Write what chlorine does in water**

Chlorine does not remain as dissolved $\text{Cl}_2$. It reacts with water in a disproportionation reaction.

Chemical equation:
$$\text{Cl}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{HCl} + \text{HClO}$$

**Look at the two acids formed**

$\text{HCl}$ is a strong acid and fully ionises to $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$. $\text{HClO}$, chloric(I) acid, is a weak acid and partly dissociates.

Dissociation:
$$\text{HClO} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{OCl}^-$$

**Pick the killer species**

The $\text{Cl}^-$ ion is very stable and has no oxidising power, so it cannot kill bacteria. The hypochlorite ion, $\text{OCl}^-$, is a powerful oxidising agent that attacks and destroys bacteria and other microbes.

options.A: Incorrect. $\text{ClO}_2^-$ is the chlorite ion and is not formed when $\text{Cl}_2$ reacts with water. Students sometimes confuse it with chlorine species because of the similar formula.
options.B: Incorrect. $\text{Cl}^-$ is the chloride ion formed from $\text{HCl}$. It is very stable with a full octet and has no oxidising ability, so it cannot disinfect water.
options.C: Incorrect. $\text{HCl}$ is a strong acid produced in the reaction, but its role is just to provide $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$. It is not the oxidising disinfectant that kills bacteria.
options.D: Correct. $\text{OCl}^-$, the hypochlorite (chlorate(I)) ion, comes from dissociation of $\text{HClO}$. It is a strong oxidiser and is the active species that kills bacteria in chlorinated water.
